Article Title: A master of mat, he now helps build India’s wrestling muscle
Article Text:
Wrestler-coach Satpal at his Rohini residence

Renowned wrestler-coach Satpal recalls the time he would participate in

dangals

near the Jama Masjid area and how he came to own a collection of 80 hats





“Whom do you want to meet?” asks the watchman at the upscale neighbourhood in Rohini’s Sector-23, looking up from his mobile. Our answer, “Pahelwan-ji”, neither illuminates nor satisfies him. “Which Pahelwan-ji?” he shoots back, reeling out three-four names. But the name “Satpal” changes his tone.“Pahelwan to bahut hain, par mahabali to ek hi hai (There are many wrestlers, but only one mighty wrestler),” he says with reverence.We wait for Satpal in a sitting room that’s bigger than a badminton court, a golden mace glowing in a corner. He appears shortly, wearing a blue kurta and lungi — and a black fedora. “I was gifted my first hat by a fencing official during the 2008 Beijing Olympics,” he says.Over the years, hats have become Satpal’s signature. His collection of 80 includes some from Australia, England, Indonesia and countries he doesn’t recollect.Professionally, however, Satpal has primarily worn two hats: of wrestler and coach. As a wrestler, he won multiple medals for India. As a coach, he has trained the likes of Yogeshwar Dutt, Bajrang Punia, Sushil Kumar (also his son-in-law), Ravi Dahiya and Aman Sehrawat, all Olympic medal-winners.“I have invested my life in wrestling,” he says.At 71, the venerated coach still cuts an imposing figure. It’s hard to believe that he was once a skinny boy who was roughed up by fellow students in Class 5. “When my father, a wrestler himself, heard about the incident, he ordered me to the village akhara,” Satpal recalls. The young boy was asked to grapple with other kids. Everyone felt he was a natural at the sport.Like most parents, Satpal’s, too, wanted him to be an engineer or a doctor. But the Bawana-born had already been bitten by the wrestling bug. After much persuasion, his father agreed to send him to Guru Hanuman’s akhara, but he set one condition: “Don’t leave your pursuit midway, else you will be grazing cattle.”It was the late Sixties. The akhara, near Amba cinema in north Delhi, had only three full-time students, Satpal recalls. One was Sudesh Kumar, who had finished sixth in the 1968 Mexico Olympics. “There was no electricity and no tap water. I used the toilets made for the labourers at the nearby Birla Mills. To avoid the queue, I would go at 4am,” he remembers.For the fledgling grappler, it was a lonely life. He would go to sleep under a sheesham (rosewood) tree and often weep. “I felt better after making friends with the children of sweepers and workers,” he says. Every month, Satpal would receive Rs 10 for provisions. And, every day, he would collect milk sent from home at Ghanta Ghar, he says. Apart from exercising and training, his morning regime included cleaning and watering the akhara.“I loved it. I believe in what Guru ji (Hanuman) used to say: ‘Agar akhaare ki sewa karoge, to tumhe phal milega (You’ll reap the rewards if you serve the akhara.)’”At 13, Satpal started appearing for the weekly dangals near Jama Masjid, which drew lively crowds. “On the first day, I won all four bouts and received Rs 10 as prize money, which improved my finances,” he says.“I must have fought over 500 bouts there. I was given the title ‘Nausherwan’, after winning on nine consecutive Sundays,” he recalls. He also remembers BJP leader Atal Bihari Vajpayee bringing a sack of almonds for the wrestlers.Satpal’s rise was meteoric. Experts recognised him as a special young talent following his impressive displays at School Games and National Championships. The 17-year-old was selected for the 1972 Munich Olympics in the men’s freestyle 62 kgs category. “I was the youngest in the contingent,” he says. He has vivid memories of the terror strike in the Games village by pro-Palestine group Black September, which left 11 Israeli athletes and coaches dead.“The Israelis were staying in flats behind ours. The attack shook everyone,” he says.Satpal also participated in the Montreal 1976 and Moscow 1980 Olympics. “During a bout in Moscow with a Czechoslovakian, I received a cut above my right eye. The repair took 16 sutures,” he says, showing the scar.The wrestler’s finest moment came at the 1982 New Delhi Asian Games , the day India lost 7-1 to Pakistan in hockey. Under the open skies, the local boy defeated his Mongolian opponent 4-0 on points before PM Indira Gandhi, sending the packed Ambedkar Stadium into raptures. “A year earlier, I had suffered a ligament tear in my right knee. I didn’t allow my rival to take advantage of that,” he remembers.The wrestler received a flat in Shalimar Bagh and about Rs 8 lakh in cash, roughly Rs 1.7 crore today.In his prime, Satpal was a synonym for box-office in rural and small-town Maharashtra. Ticketed contests in towns like Kolhapur, Belgaum, Hubli and Poona were attended by thousands who loved his famous ‘hathi chingharh daav’ (screaming elephant move). Satpal would be mobbed by adoring spectators and adorned with currency garlands, and was later crowned ‘Rustom-e-Hind’.Satpal, who served as a senior sports officer for the Delhi govt, continues to train wrestlers at the Chhatrasal Stadium. A recipient of the Arjuna and Dronacharya awards as well as the Padma Bhushan, he believes that Tokyo Asian Games gold medal winners Sujeet Kalkal and Aman Sherawat are good bets for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.Not many know that the wrestling guru also played the lead in a hit Haryanvi film, ‘Premi Ramphal’, in 1985. “I got more acting offers. But if I had accepted them, the Olympic medals (of my wards) may not have come,” he says.Satpal knows which hat suits him most.
Article Summary: At 71, wrestler-coach Satpal still cuts an imposing figure. He has trained the likes of Yogeshwar Dutt, Bajrang Punia, Sushil Kumar, Ravi Dahiya and Aman Sehrawat. His collection of 80 hats includes some from Australia, England, Indonesia.

Article Title: Class XII Delhi student found burnt in Shahdara school, police probe on
Article Text:
An 18-year-old Class XII student was found burned behind her school, stirring suspicions of suicide





NEW DELHI: A Class XII student allegedly set herself ablaze behind the guard room of a govt school in east Delhi ’s Shahdara Saturday, with police suspecting suicide. Police sources said an alleged note had been found at the spot.Police received a PCR call about a fire at the school and rushed to the spot, where the 18-year-old student was found in a severely burnt condition. She was pronounced dead at a hospital. An empty bottle and the student’s school bag were found at the spot.Police sources said investigators were probing all angles, including her academic records, family circumstances and a possible relationship. A senior officer refused to comment on the contents of the note, saying they are being examined to establish their authenticity.The student apparently left her classroom after a lesson, saying she was going to drink water. Two to three minutes later, screams were heard, and she was found severely burnt near the tank. Asked to confirm these details, a police officer said the matter was under investigation and the circumstances leading to the incident were yet to be established.Police suspect she might have brought a flammable substance to school in the bottle found near her.A crime team has collected evidence from the spot.A fire official said they received information around 11.58am that a student had allegedly set herself on fire inside the school. “We found the student in a burnt condition behind a water tank. Her face was completely burnt,” he said.The girl’s elder sister told reporters that she and their niece had dropped the girl at school and she appeared happy. “She was laughing when she went inside. I don’t know what happened after that,” the elder sister said, breaking down in tears.She added that she had received a call from the school around 12.40pm, informing her that something serious had happened. Another relative said she reached the school around 1pm and got to know about the incident.The girl’s uncle raised suspicions of a foul play and questioned why her school bag was not checked. He said her parents had gone to Koderma in Jharkhand following her maternal grandmother’s death. “It is impossible that she could have set herself on fire. She was a good student and was not facing any issues. False information was being spread about her,” he said.The uncle wondered how the incident could have gone unnoticed despite CCTV cameras and staff’s presence at the school. He also alleged that the family was informed late and demanded that the possibility of another person being involved should be investigated.Education minister Ashish Sood, who visited the school, said police were investigating the incident and the school was cooperating with them. “It is a deeply tragic incident... The school has submitted all relevant evidence to police... We request some time for the investigation to proceed. Further details will be shared once the investigation is complete,” he said.
Article Summary: An 18-year-old Class XII student was found burned behind her school, stirring suspicions of suicide. The student apparently left her classroom after a lesson, saying she was going to drink water. Two to three minutes later, screams were heard, and she was found severely burnt.

Article Title: De-Stress mantra: Reimagining Van Gogh’s Starry Night
Article Text:
Let's D-Stress event at Starbucks, Aerocity in New Delhi on Saturday

The

Times of India

’s





New Delhi: What if Vincent van Gogh’s iconic ‘The Starry Night’ had a yellow sky instead of its swirling blues, or its familiar landscape gave way to a green grassland? At a sip-and-paint session in Aerocity Saturday, participants were encouraged to set aside the rules of art and give their own interpretations to the 19th-century masterpiece, one brushstroke at a time.From children painting alongside their parents to adults immersing themselves in colours, participants atLet’s D-Stress session at Starbucks Reserve in Aerocity explored art as a way to unwind. With pre-drawn canvases, colour palettes and painting essentials laid out for them, they were free to experiment with colours and express themselves as visual artist Pavani Nagpal K Chhabra and her team moved around the room, offering guidance on brushstrokes and painting techniques.Participants soon became engrossed in their canvases, sipping coffee and enjoying snacks as they worked on their versions of the famous painting. The idea was not to reproduce the original, but to let imagination take over.For Nagpal, who led the workshop, art has been a source of freedom and happiness since childhood. “Since childhood, I always wanted to be an artist. I used to feel the most free, loved and happiest whenever I had a paintbrush in my hand.”Explaining how painting can help people de-stress, she said art offers a medium through which people can express feelings that may otherwise remain unspoken. “It is a mode of expression where everybody is free to express their inner feelings on a canvas, which helps them let it out. It is a medium where they can also set their imaginations free. It is a great exercise to engage in, pouring out emotions on the canvas and helping themselves de-stress or feel relieved. ”Nagpal said the choice of painting was deliberate. While ‘The Starry Night’, painted in 1889, is among the most recognisable works in modern art, Van Gogh’s personal struggles and pursuit of art on his own terms resonated with the theme of the session.“Why we chose this painting for the de-stress event is because ‘The Starry Night’ is one of the most iconic paintings that everybody knows about. But throughout his life, Van Gogh couldn’t sell his work. He did not paint for anybody’s validation or to earn money; he just did it for his heart,” she said. “Art is something that comes from the heart, and one enjoys doing it. There is no math, no formula. Your sky could be any colour you want. ”The session also saw young participants discovering their interest in painting. Four-year-old Zaira Sethia, who attended with her mother, now wants to become an artist when she grows up.Alongside the art workshop, attendees were introduced to Starbucks’ festive coffee range. They were also guided through the process of smelling and tasting coffee, exploring how its aromas and flavours can be experienced beyond simply drinking a cup.
Article Summary: Let’s D-Stress session at Starbucks Reserve in Aerocity explored art as a way to unwind. Participants were encouraged to set aside the rules of art and give their own interpretations to the 19th-century masterpiece, one brushstroke at a time.
